title: Unlocking Currency Conversion in SQLScript with CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA and Datasphere
author: pradeep_gupta1
text:
Currency conversion is a common requirement in SAP reporting, analytics, pricing, and planning scenarios. Whether you are developing SQLScript Table Functions in SAP HANA XSA, building reusable data models in SAP HANA Cloud, or creating analytical models in SAP Datasphere, you will eventually need to compare and report data maintained in multiple currencies. 
 SAP provides the built-in CONVERT_CURRENCY() function to perform currency conversion directly within SQL. Rather than implementing custom exchange rate logic, developers can leverage SAP's standard currency conversion framework and exchange rate tables. 
 This article provides a practical overview of how to use CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA and SAP Datasphere, along with some implementation patterns that I've found useful in real-world projects. 
 If You Have Already Used Currency Conversion in Calculation Views... 
 If you've previously configured Currency Conversion for a measure within the Semantics node of a HANA Calculation View, many of the concepts used by CONVERT_CURRENCY() will already be familiar. 

 Both approaches rely on the same fundamental business concepts: 
 Amount 
 Source Currency 
 Target Currency 
 Exchange Rate Type 
 Reference Date 
 The primary difference is that Calculation Views expose these settings through a graphical interface, whereas CONVERT_CURRENCY() provides direct access through SQLScript. 
 Basic Syntax 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => NET_VALUE,
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => SALES_CURRENCY,
 "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
 "CLIENT" => '500',
 "SCHEMA" => 'MY_SCHEMA'
) 
 The function converts the amount from the source currency into the target currency using the exchange rate configuration defined in the SAP currency conversion framework. 
 Most Common Parameters 
 Although the function supports a large number of parameters, most implementations typically use the following: 
 AMOUNT – Monetary value to be converted 
 SOURCE_UNIT – Source currency 
 TARGET_UNIT – Reporting currency 
 REFERENCE_DATE – Date used to determine the exchange rate 
 CONVERSION_TYPE – Exchange rate type (for example M, P, or B) 
 ERROR_HANDLING – Controls behavior when exchange rates cannot be determined 
 Additional parameters are available for specifying the underlying currency conversion tables, which is especially relevant for HDI Container-based implementations. 
 Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA 
 One practical use case involved reporting SAP pricing conditions in a common currency. Pricing records were maintained globally using multiple currencies, but the business required global reporting in USD. 
 The following example converts a pricing condition value into USD: 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => "KBETR",
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => "KONWA",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
 "CLIENT" => '500',
 "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) AS "KBETR_USD" 
 This provides a standardized price regardless of the original currency in which the pricing condition was maintained. 
 Working with HDI Containers 
 Many SAP HANA XSA projects expose SAP currency tables through synonyms rather than directly accessing the underlying TCUR* tables. 
 Typical examples include: 
 TCURR_CV_SYN
TCURF_CV_SYN
TCURV_CV_SYN
TCURN_CV_SYN
TCURX_CV_SYN 
 In these scenarios, the synonym objects can be passed directly into CONVERT_CURRENCY(): 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => "KBETR",
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => "KONWA",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
 "CLIENT" => '500',
 "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null',
 "CONFIGURATION_TABLE" => 'TCURV_CV_SYN',
 "PRECISIONS_TABLE" => 'TCURX_CV_SYN',
 "NOTATIONS_TABLE" => 'TCURN_CV_SYN',
 "RATES_TABLE" => 'TCURR_CV_SYN',
 "PREFACTORS_TABLE" => 'TCURF_CV_SYN'
) 
 This is a common pattern in HDI Container-based applications where SAP ERP or S/4HANA metadata is exposed through synonyms. 
 Combining Unit Conversion and Currency Conversion 
 In many pricing scenarios, comparing currencies alone is not sufficient. Prices may also be maintained using different pricing units or units of measure. 
 In one implementation, the pricing condition was first normalized into a common reporting unit: 
 K."KBETR" * (UN."UMREZ" / UN."UMREN") 
 The normalized value was then converted into USD: 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => K."KBETR" * (UN."UMREZ" / UN."UMREN"),
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => K."KONWA",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
 "CLIENT" => '500',
 "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) 
 This produces pricing values that are comparable across: 
 Multiple currencies 
 Different pricing units 
 Different units of measure 
 Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP Datasphere SQL Views 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY() is not limited to SAP HANA XSA. Developers working with SAP Datasphere can also use the function directly within SQL Views running in SQLScript mode. 
 For example: 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => "GROSS_SALES_VALUE",
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => "SALES_CURRENCY",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => "SALES_DATE",
 "CLIENT" => '100',
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) 
 This approach provides full flexibility for implementing custom currency conversion logic directly inside Datasphere SQL models. 
 Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in Datasphere Graphical Views 
 One capability that is easy to overlook is that developers are not limited to using CONVERT_CURRENCY() within SQL Views. SAP Datasphere also allows the function to be embedded directly within Calculated Columns in Graphical Views. 
 For example: 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => "GROSS_SALES_VALUE",
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => "SALES_CURRENCY",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => :P_REPORTING_CURRENCY,
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => :P_EXCHANGE_RATE_DATE,
 "CLIENT" => '500',
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) 
 This combines the simplicity of graphical modelling with the flexibility of parameter-driven currency conversion. Business users can dynamically choose reporting currencies and exchange-rate dates without modifying the model itself. 
 Making Currency Conversion Dynamic 
 Hardcoding target currencies and dates may be suitable for some reporting scenarios, but many business users require flexibility. 
 By utilizing input parameters, the same logic can support multiple reporting currencies: 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY(
 "AMOUNT" => "NET_REVENUE",
 "SOURCE_UNIT" => "DOCUMENT_CURRENCY",
 "TARGET_UNIT" => :P_TARGET_CURRENCY,
 "REFERENCE_DATE" => :P_RATE_DATE,
 "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
 "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) 
 This pattern works particularly well in SAP Datasphere analytical models and parameter-driven reporting scenarios. 
 Conclusion 
 CONVERT_CURRENCY() is a useful built-in function available across SAP HANA XSA, SAP HANA Cloud, and SAP Datasphere. Whether you're building SQLScript Table Functions, SQL Views, or Graphical Views, the function provides a consistent and flexible way to perform currency conversion using SAP's standard currency conversion framework. 
 By understanding the core parameters, HDI Container considerations, and Datasphere integration options, developers can significantly reduce the effort required to implement robust currency conversion logic across enterprise reporting and analytical solutions.

title: What Drives It All: The Compliance Data Foundation in SAP S/4HANA for Product Compliance
author: Eva_Sch
text:
This post builds on and complements a previous article in which we introduced the three core capabilities of SAP S/4HANA for Product Compliance. If you haven't read the blog post “Product Compliance in SAP S/4HANA: How Three Integrated Capabilities Enable Safe Global Operations” yet, you can find it here: Product Compliance in SAP S/4HANA: How Three Integrated Capabilities Enable Safe Global Operations 
 In this post, we go one level deeper and take a closer look at what drives all three capabilities: the Compliance Data Foundation . 

 This foundation is your single source of truth for regulatory execution. At its core: Compliance Requirements, Purposes, and Content that work together across three key capabilities: Product Marketability & Component Compliance, Dangerous Goods Management and Compliance Document Management. 
 The already mentioned Compliance Requirements are the semantic anchor, and deliverable building blocks that capture the obligations from a regulation, part of a regulation, or a stakeholder requirement. Think of examples like "Labeling according to GHS," or "Dangerous Goods Classification according to ADN or IATA." 
 Compliance Requirements are assigned to a product through Compliance Purposes which are self-configurable bundles that group the relevant compliance requirements based on a specific obligation a company needs to fulfill. A Compliance Purpose can be created for a country, a region, a customer group, a product type, or a business process. They are highly flexible and can be defined however your use case demands. 
 And here is what makes the Compliance Data Foundation so powerful: 
 When regulations change , the update flows through the foundation straight into execution , no manual intervention across multiple places. 
 The result? Consistent, audit-ready compliance logic that scales with your business and keeps pace with an ever-evolving regulatory landscape.

title: Generating Microsoft Word .docx from ABAP Cloud (S/4HANA Public Edition) — Let Word Do the Rendering
author: cuongus
text:
On S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition you can generate real Microsoft Word documents from ABAP without parsing or rewriting word/document.xml . Instead of making ABAP render the document, you let Word render it: the template carries Content Controls bound to a Custom XML Part, and the engine swaps exactly one file inside the .docx ZIP. 
 The result is a compact ABAP Cloud class built only on released APIs, plus a template repository app where business users upload and maintain their own Word templates. 
 This post covers the approach, the released APIs I verified on the tenant, the ABAP that does the work, and — most importantly — the OOXML traps that cost me the most debugging time. It ends with an experiment showing why the very same trick cannot be used for Excel.

title: BAS Preview: OData V2 POST fails with 403 CSRF token validation failed
author: alexpi007
text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 I am using SAP BTP Trial and SAP Business Application Studio. 
 I have a SAP Fiori Elements List Report/Object Page application using OData V2. 
 Environment: 
 - SAP BTP Trial 
 - SAP Business Application Studio 
 - Dev Space: SAP Fiori 
 - UI5 version in BAS Preview: 1.152.0 
 - OData service: /sap/opu/odata/sap/ZUI_PIA_ORDER_O2/ 
 - Entity set: ZC_PIA_ORDER 
 Problem: 
 The application works correctly when deployed as an HTML5 Application and launched through BTP Launchpad. The Create operation works successfully there. 
 However, the same application running in BAS Preview cannot create an entity. 
 Read requests work correctly: 
 - OData service root: HTTP 200 
 - $metadata: HTTP 200 
 - Vendor Value Help: HTTP 200 
 Create fails: 
 POST /sap/opu/odata/sap/ZUI_PIA_ORDER_O2/ZC_PIA_ORDER 
 Response: 
 - HTTP 403 Forbidden 
 - X-CSRF-Token: Required 
 - Response body: "CSRF token validation failed" 
 The important point is that the POST request DOES contain an X-CSRF-Token request header. The BAS session cookie is also sent. 
 Troubleshooting performed: 
 1. Restarted the BAS Dev Space. 
 2. Executed: 
 curl http://localhost:8887/reload 
 3. Cleared BAS Preview site data/cookies and authenticated again. 
 4. Started a fresh BAS Preview session. 
 5. Verified that the CSRF token is present in the POST request. 
 6. Checked request cookies. 
 7. Checked for the ARBE cookie; it is not present. 
 8. The issue remains reproducible after a clean Preview session. 
 9. The OData model uses "useBatch": false. 
 10. The same Create operation works successfully in the deployed BTP HTML5 Application. 
 The failing POST response contains: 
 - HTTP 403 Forbidden 
 - X-CSRF-Token: Required 
 - Server: sap-business-application-studio 
 - No Set-Cookie response header 
 Could this be a BAS Preview proxy/session/CSRF token synchronization issue? 
 This looks similar to the BAS CSRF issues described in SAP KBA 3400009 and KBA 3730925. 
 Could anyone from SAP BAS/Fiori tools team advise whether there is a current workaround or known issue?

title: URGENT CIC ESCALATION: Technical Grading Failure on C_TS452 System-Based Exam (Static Score 72.86%)
author: zerihun
text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 I am posting to raise awareness and ask if anyone else has experienced a technical issue with the SAP Certified Application Associate – Sourcing and Procurement (C_TS452) System-Based Assessment (SyBA). 
 The Issue 
 During recent attempts on the same day, after making extensive corrections to task-level activities (master data configuration, purchasing setups, and transactional postings like GR/MIRO), the assessment repeatedly returned an identical score of 72.86% . 
 Even more concerning, a colleague from our organization completed an independent attempt with different workflow corrections, and received the exact same score percentage (72.86%) down to the decimal point. 
 Why This Indicates a Systemic / Platform Issue 
 Given that the task execution differed significantly across these attempts, receiving the exact same score strongly points toward a backend platform defect rather than a candidate error. Specifically: 

 Cached Tenant Snapshots: The evaluation engine may be pulling from a frozen, cached snapshot instead of querying live database updates. 

 Script Execution Exceptions: The background automated grading script may be hitting an uncaught exception on specific user profiles, halting early and defaulting to a static baseline score. 

 Environment Caching: Same-day re-attempts might not be refreshing dynamic tenant namespaces properly between sessions. 
 Current Status & Questions for the Community 

 We have logged an official support ticket and escalated via the Customer Interaction Center (CIC) to request a technical log audit for our P-IDs. 

 Has anyone in the community encountered static/identical scores across different attempts on S/4HANA system-based exams recently? 

 How long did SAP Certification Operations take to audit backend evaluation scripts and restore affected attempt credits in your case? 
 Any insights from community mentors, SAP Education representatives, or fellow candidates who faced similar SyBA evaluation glitches would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thank you!

title: Coming Soon: A Smarter, More Transparent Feedback Experience
author: Florian Heretsch
text:
At SAP, customer feedback has always been part of how we build our software. Our first products were developed in close collaboration with customers, and that same principle is still true today: we need to listen, understand the context, and turn feedback into product improvements that create real value. 

 The challenge is not whether we receive enough feedback—we receive a lot of it. The real challenge is making sure feedback reaches the right teams, with the right context, so it can create impact and customers can see where it goes. 

 What’s changing 

 On October 6, 2026 , we are launching an enhanced Customer Influence experience, making feedback easier to submit, easier to follow from submission to resolution, and easier for SAP teams to act on. We’re also improving our feedback ecosystem by connecting customer feedback, usage insights, research, and market signals, so we can make better-informed decisions across SAP products. 
 From feedback to innovation in the SAP feedback ecosystem 

 Simpler access to customer influence 

 Soon, it will be easier than ever to dive into influencing SAP products via Customer Influence. S-users will find the feedback tool in the SAP for Me portal they already know, while P-users will enjoy direct access to the feedback system via an updated influence.sap.com . 

 A more intuitive experience 

 More intuitive navigation helps remove friction from the process while clear visibility into outcomes shows how your input drives innovation. 
 Real-time view of request status and voting 

 How it works 

 Advances in AI, automation, and real-time data processing create an opportunity to work with feedback differently than in the past. Now we can identify patterns and route feedback to the right teams faster and at a much greater scale. Individual signals become collective insight that drives more meaningful, relevant improvements grounded in real-world feedback. That means our experts can spend less time processing information and more time acting on it and delivering outcomes that matter to your business. 

 Meanwhile, consistent, company-wide guidelines bring a standardized approach to handling, responding to, and acting on feedback across SAP’s portfolio, tools, processes, and teams. 

 While AI helps us meet customer needs more efficiently, people remain accountable for understanding the context, making prioritization decisions, and deciding what we build. That is important because feedback is not only data. It reflects human experiences behind real business challenges, and it takes human judgment to turn those signals into outcomes that genuinely matter. 

 What changes for you 

 These enhancements are about clear value—not replacing what works. All five Customer Influence services you know today continue within the improved feedback experience. For example, in SAP Continuous Influence, you can find your existing improvement requests in the new experience and use any existing bookmark links you have. 

 Here’s what you can expect: 

 Effortless feedback experience : simplified navigation, a more intuitive journey, and direct feedback service access for SAP for Me users 

 Clearer line of sight : transparency from submission to resolution, with progress tracking at every step and consistent updates 

 More influence : greater visibility into how your feedback shapes the SAP road map and contributes to product improvements 

 The right products : unified feedback, market analysis, and user research helping SAP deliver more of what matters most 

 The conversation continues 

 The momentum doesn’t stop here. We’re also exploring agentic assistance that helps customers structure feedback, suggests clearer wording, and guides them toward the most impactful way to share what they’re experiencing—making the act of sharing feedback feel less like a task and more like a conversation. 

 As the relaunch of Customer Influence approaches, look for more information about the release on influence.sap.com, including access and enablement resources. 

 In the meantime, you can explore current Customer Influence services and continue submitting your feedback at influence.sap.com . 

 This is a next step, not a final one—we are still building, and the feedback you continue to share will help us get this right.

title: SAP and NVIDIA OpenShell: Working Toward Governance and Security for Auditable AI Agents in Enterprise Systems
author: Andre Lamego
text:
Together with NVIDIA, SAP is helping shape and strengthen the execution layer for enterprise agentic AI. 
 The new AI-first experience for building agents, apps, and workflows 

 Meet Joule Studio 

 Today, alongside the announcement of NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform and the broad availability of NVIDIA OpenShell, we’re deepening our collaboration with NVIDIA to help make enterprise AI agents safer, more governable, and easier to audit by design. 

 As announced this year at SAP Sapphire , SAP and NVIDIA have a deep technical collaboration, with plans to bring SAP Business AI Platform together with OpenShell, an open-source secure runtime for autonomous AI agents. This is more than a planned integration, it reflects a shared effort to help define what “enterprise-grade” means for autonomous AI systems. 

 As part of our ongoing co-development activities, SAP engineers are contributing directly to the OpenShell codebase and embedding OpenShell within SAP Business AI Platform. Joule Studio , an AI-first development environment, provides a complete execution and governance stack for enterprise AI agents, while OpenShell supports deploying agents with a focus on safety and security. 

 SAP and NVIDIA are also working to: 

 Help harden the OpenShell runtime for enterprise-scale deployment, including in regulated industries with strict security and compliance requirements 

 Connect OpenShell’s runtime isolation with the business governance layer of Joule Studio runtime, linking technical execution boundaries to enterprise authorization models, IAM frameworks, and audit trails 

 Work toward FedRAMP, FIPS, and regulated-industry enablement on a committed road map 

 Advance open research and AI safety through the Open Secure AI Alliance , of which SAP and NVIDIA are both founding members alongside other industry leaders 

 Joule Studio runtime: Governance above the execution layer 

 Joule Studio runtime helps determine whether an action should execute at all—applying business authorization, role-based policy, and process context before a request in action reaches the runtime. OpenShell provides an open-source runtime boundary designed to help build and deploy autonomous, self-evolving agents more safely. It governs how the agent executes, what it can see and do, and where inference goes. Together, the two aim to give enterprise customers execution containment and business accountability in a single integrated stack. 

 SAP engineering contributions to NVIDIA OpenShell 

 SAP engineers are contributing to four areas of the OpenShell project. On platform architecture, SAP has helped drive decomposition of the runtime into independently deployable components, separating the supervisor and agent execution layers so they can scale independently. For Kubernetes-native operations, contributions include operator support, image pull secret management for private container registries, custom volume claim templates, and foreground deletion of sandbox resources. SAP has also worked to minimize the gateway image footprint and extend compute driver support for heterogeneous enterprise infrastructure. Contributions to supervisor health monitoring and structured log-level configuration bring the runtime to enterprise observability standards. 

 Joule Studio runtime is available free for SAP customers and partners through October 2026— start building today

title: SAP BTP Destinations: Configuration for Different Service Types
author: Myvizhipriya_Thangaraj_2810
text:
Overview: 
 In the previous blog ( SAP BTP Destinations: Understanding the Basics ), we covered the basics of SAP BTP Destinations and why they are essential for connecting BTP applications with external systems. 
 Now, let’s get into the scenarios you’ll actually encounter in real projects. 
 Not all destinations are configured the same way. The setup depends on where you’re connecting, how the system is exposed, and what authentication it requires. 
 For example, connecting to S/4HANA Cloud is different from connecting to an on-premise S/4HANA system . And when you’re working with an external REST API, you may need a completely different authentication setup. 
 So, in this blog, we’ll break down the most common SAP BTP destination scenarios, what makes each one different, and the key configurations you need to get them working. 
 Let's have a quick look on the streamlining BTP Connectivity with Destinations before deep diving it individually: 

 Picture 1: BTP Connectivity with Destination 

 Different Types of Services: 
 1. S/4HANA Cloud 
 When a BTP application needs to consume APIs from S/4HANA Cloud, we generally create an HTTP destination pointing to the S/4HANA API endpoint. 
 A typical OAuth 2.0 client credentials configuration looks like: // Client credentials configuration
Name: S4HANA_CLOUD
Type: HTTP
URL: <S/4HANA API URL>
Proxy Type: Internet
Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials 
 as next, Client ID: <client-id>
Client Secret: <client-secret>
Token Service URL: <token-endpoint> 
 The exact endpoint and authentication details depend on the API and the configuration on the S/4HANA Cloud side. 
 The important thing is to make sure that the OAuth client configured in S/4HANA Cloud has the required permissions to access the API. 
 So the overall flow becomes: 
 BTP Application -> Destination -> S/4HANA Cloud API 

 2. S/4HANA On-Premise 
 The configuration changes when our S/4HANA system is running inside the corporate network . 
 In this case, SAP Cloud Connector is commonly used to establish secure connectivity between SAP BTP and the on-premise system. // The destination may look like as follows:
Name: S4HANA_ONPREM
Type: HTTP
URL: http://<virtual-host>:<port>
Proxy Type: OnPremise
Authentication: <authentication-method> 
 Here, the URL configured in the destination is typically based on the virtual host and port defined in Cloud Connector. 
 The connectivity flow is: 
 BTP Application -> Destination -> Connectivity Service -> Cloud Connector -> S/4HANA On-Premise 
 This means there are actually two configurations to consider: 
 Destination configuration in BTP 
 Cloud Connector configuration for the backend system 
 If either one is incorrect, the application will not be able to reach the backend. 

 3. SAP Integration Suite / Cloud Integration 
 Another common scenario is calling an integration flow deployed in SAP Integration Suite. 
 For example, an iFlow may expose an HTTPS endpoint that needs to be consumed by a BTP application. // A typical destination looks like as follows:
Name: CPI_IFLOW
Type: HTTP
URL: <iFlow endpoint>
Proxy Type: Internet
Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials 
 as next, Client ID: <client-id>
Client Secret: <client-secret>
Token Service URL: <token-endpoint> 
 The authentication configured in the destination must match what is configured for the integration endpoint. 
 The advantage here is that the BTP application does not need to manage the iFlow URL and authentication details directly. 

 4. SAP SaaS Services 
 The same destination concept can be used when connecting BTP applications to SAP cloud services such as SuccessFactors, Ariba, Concur, and other SaaS solutions. 
 For example: Name: SAP_SAAS_API
Type: HTTP
URL: <API endpoint>
Proxy Type: Internet
Authentication: <supported authentication> 
 The authentication mechanism depends on the individual service. 
 Some services may use OAuth 2.0, while others may support Basic Authentication, certificates, or other mechanisms. 
 This is why it is important to first understand the authentication model supported by the target service before creating the destination. 

 5. External REST API (Most common way) 
 Destinations are also commonly used for non-SAP systems. 
 Let's say our BTP application needs to consume an external REST API. 
 For an API using OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials: // Client Credentials as follows:
Name: EXTERNAL_REST_API
Type: HTTP
URL: https://api.example.com
Proxy Type: Internet
Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials 
 as next, Client ID: <client-id>
Client Secret: <client-secret>
Token Service URL: <token-endpoint> 
 For an API using Basic Authentication, the configuration would instead use the authentication method supported by that API. 
 The important point is that the destination configuration should always follow the authentication requirements of the external service. Best Example: Northwind OData Services 

 6. Principal Propagation 
 In some enterprise scenarios, simply using a technical user or client credentials is not enough. 
 We may need to forward the identity of the logged-in BTP user to the backend system. This is where Principal Propagation becomes relevant. 
 A simplified flow looks like: 
 BTP User -> BTP Application -> Destination -> Cloud Connector -> Backend System 
 This scenario requires additional identity and trust configuration across the BTP environment, Cloud Connector, and backend system. 
 Therefore, Principal Propagation should be treated as an end-to-end configuration rather than just a destination property. 

 Picture 2: Quick Overview of different services types 

 Choosing the Right Authentication 
 One of the most important decisions while creating a destination is selecting the correct authentication mechanism. 
 A simple way to think about it is: 

 Scenario 
 Common Authentication 

 S/4HANA Cloud API 
 OAuth 2.0 

 On-Premise SAP system 
 Basic / Certificate / Principal Propagation 

 Integration Suite endpoint 
 OAuth 2.0 / Basic 

 SAP SaaS API 
 OAuth 2.0 / Service-specific 

 External REST API 
 OAuth 2.0 / API Key / Basic 

 User-based backend access 
 Principal Propagation 
 These are common patterns, not fixed rules. The target service documentation and security configuration should always be the final reference. 

 Common Issues During Testing 
 Destination-related issues are often not caused by the destination itself. 
 For example, if an on-premise API is not reachable, we should check the complete connectivity chain instead of immediately changing destination properties. 

 Picture 3: Issues Impact API Connectivity 

 Some common areas to check are: 
 Incorrect URL or endpoint 
 Incorrect Proxy Type 
 Invalid credentials 
 Incorrect OAuth token endpoint 
 Missing scopes or authorizations 
 Cloud Connector configuration 
 Backend host or port configuration 
 Certificate or trust configuration 
 API permissions on the target system 
 A good troubleshooting approach is to identify where the request is failing : 
 Application -> Destination -> Connectivity -> Authentication -> Target System 
 This makes troubleshooting much more systematic. 

 Recommended Approach 
 When creating a destination for a new service, I normally follow a simple sequence as shown in the following picture: 

 Picture 4: SAP BTP Configuration and Connectivity Patterns 

 Conclusion 
 Destination configurations may vary from service to service, but the thinking behind them stays the same: 
 We need to understand: Target system → Endpoint → Connectivity → Authentication → Authorization 
 Once these pieces are clear, configuring a destination becomes much more straightforward. 
 Quick Recap 
 S/4HANA Cloud: Focus on OAuth, API access, and required permissions. 
 On-Premise Systems: Cloud Connector and network connectivity are key. 
 External APIs: The authentication approach depends on the API provider. 
 So rather than memorizing destination properties, it is better to understand the connectivity pattern behind each scenario . 
 Once we understand that connectivity pattern, you can configure destinations with confidence and troubleshoot them much faster when something goes wrong. 
 Thank you for taking the time to read this blog! If you found this helpful, i would love to hear your thoughts, feedback or questions in the comments. Let's keep learning and growing together! 
 I’m still new to blogging, so if you notice anything that could be improved or corrected, please don’t hesitate to let me know!!

title: Getting a Verification Code to Register Your Peppol Participant for Slovakia
author: anton_niko
text:
Getting a Verification Code to Register Your Peppol Participant for Slovakia 
 Note: The steps and processes described here are accurate as of the time of writing, but it's essential to stay updated with any changes on the tax authority portal or the test tool for PFS that may affect this procedure. 
 If you are a Slovakian company and you use SAP Document and Reporting Compliance, cloud edition to exchange electronic documents with your business partners and the tax authority, you must register a Peppol participant for your company as part of the setup. One of the prerequisites for creating this participant is a verification code. The verification code confirms that you have selected SAP SE as your certified delivery service provider, making SAP your access point in the Peppol network. 
 How you obtain the verification code depends on whether you use it for production or for test purposes. In this blog, you will learn how to obtain the verification code for both. 
 Obtaining the Verification Code for Production Purposes 
 For production purposes, you obtain the verification code by registering on the Slovak Financial Administration portal and selecting SAP SE as your certified delivery service provider. 
 Open the tax authority portal at https://vpds.financnasprava.sk/ . 
 Navigate to the page listing the accredited service providers. 
 Choose SAP SE as your accredited service provider and initiate the registration of your participant by selecting the corresponding action in the portal. 
 After the request has been successfully submitted, the Financial Administration sends a message to your inbox in the Personal Internet Zone (Osobná internetová zóna – OIZ). The message is titled Submission of a request for selection of a certified delivery service provider (Odoslanie žiadosti pre výber certifikovaného poskytovateľa doručovacej služby). 
 Inside this message, copy the Verification data / verification code (Verifikačný údaj): <#EncryptedData#> and use it as the verification code when creating the participant for your company for production purposes. 
 Important: If you have email notifications enabled, the notification e-mail only informs you that a new message has been delivered to your Financial Administration mailbox. The verification code itself is not included in the notification email — you must open the message directly in OIZ to retrieve it. 
 Obtaining the Verification Code for Test Purposes 
 For testing your integration with the Slovak Financial Administration's test environment (tPFS), you generate the verification code yourself using a dedicated test tool. 
 Open the Test tools for PFS (Testovacie nástroje PFS) at overtoken.sk/generate . The page provides tools for testing integration with the Slovak Financial Administration test environment (tPFS). 
 Sign in by clicking Sign in (Prihlásiť sa). If prompted, continue using the configured Google account. 
 Scroll to the section Generate a standalone verification token (data) (Vygenerovať samostatný verifikačný token (údaj)). 
 Enter the Service provider TIN for SAP (DIČ poskytovateľa služby): DE143454214 
 Enter your Entity TIN (DIČ subjektu — 10 digits). 
 Click Generate verification token (data) (Vygenerovať verifikačný token (údaj)). 
 Copy the generated verification token and use it as the verification code when creating the participant for your company for test purposes. 

 Next Step: Creating a Peppol Participant for Slovakia 
 Once you have the verification code, you can proceed to create a Peppol participant for your company in SAP Document and Reporting Compliance, cloud edition. For more information, see Creating a Participant for Your Company for Slovakia .

title: What is planned for the 2611 release of SAP Variant Configuration and Pricing?
author: Michael_W141
text:
The 2611 release of SAP Variant Configuration and Pricing is planned to be deployed to BTP customer tenants on October 21, 2026 : 
 Administration UI and Administration service:

 This blog covers the following planned innovations: 
 Pricing service - Price Agreement Data in Stateless Pricing Response 
 Pricing service - Alternate Product Units Accessible in Pricing Extension Interface 
 Pricing service - Parent Item Access in Pricing Extension Interface

 It also includes a call to act regarding the following changes: 
 Administration - Load Changed Variant Tables Only 

 Please check the updated roadmap and release notes after the release date to see which of these features were delivered as planned.

 Pricing service - Price Agreement Data in Stateless Pricing Response 
 A new value items-priceAgreement for the optional query parameter $select has been introduced for the stateless pricing endpoint. This enhancement enables callers to retrieve price agreement details alongside the pricing results. 
 Usage: POST /api/v1/statelesspricing?$select=items-priceAgreement 
 When multiple price agreements with different validities exist for the same condition type, the pricing engine selects one at runtime for calculation. Previously, the stateless response did not include price agreement data, making it impossible for callers to identify which agreement was applied. 
 Only when items-priceAgreement is requested, the response includes the price agreement details used during calculation for each item. This provides full transparency into which price agreement was selected and applied, enabling consuming applications to display accurate pricing information to end users. 
 More information will be published with the November release in the API Definition and the Development Guide (Pre-Production). 

 Pricing service - Alternate Product Units Accessible in Pricing Extension Interface 
 The pricing extension input interface has been enhanced to receive alternate product units from the pricing input payload, enabling custom routines to perform high-precision unit conversions during pricing calculation. 
 During quantity conversion, rounding errors may occur because the condition base is limited to 3 decimal places. When the sales unit and condition unit differ, the resulting condition base is truncated to 3 decimal places - causing discrepancies between the expected and actual calculated values. 
 SAP Note 22963 describes a formula-based workaround to perform the conversion at full precision using the numerator and denominator from the unit of measure conversion table (MARM in the back-end). Since MARM is not replicated, the only viable source for these values at runtime is the pricing input payload itself. 
 Previously, alternate product units present in the pricing input payload were not passed through to the extension interface, making it impossible for custom formulas to implement this workaround. 
 With this enhancement, alternate product units supplied in the pricing input payload under productDetails.alternateProductUnits are now accessible within the pricing extension interface at runtime. Custom local routines can read the numerator and denominator values directly during formula execution to perform the full-precision conversion without intermediate rounding. 
 More information will be published with the November release in the Extension Guide (Pre-Production). 

 Pricing service - Parent Item Access in Pricing Extension Interface 
 The pricing extension input interface has been enhanced to receive the parent item- and root item context, enabling custom formulas to implement cross-item pricing logic based on higher-level line item data. 
 When a pricing formula was executed for a condition of a child item, the extension interface only provided access to the current item's context. There was no way to navigate to the parent item from within the formula - making it impossible to implement pricing patterns where a child item's value depends on a condition of its higher-level item. 
 Example: 
 A main item has a condition value of 10,000.00 USD calculated at the document level 
 A child item has a percentage-based condition with a rate of 7.5% 
 Expected: child item base = condition value of parent item -> child item value = 10,000.00 x 7.5% = 750.00 USD 
 The pricing formula interface now exposes access to the parent item and root item from within a child item formula execution. Custom formulas can: 
 Navigate to the parent item or root item from the current item context 
 Read item-level data of the parent item 
 Use parent condition values as the base for child item calculations 
 More information will be published with the November release in the Extension Guide (Pre-Production). 

 Pricing service - Application Filter and Language Filter on Condition Type GET Endpoint 
 The GET endpoint for condition types has been enhanced with an optional application query parameter and a new $select=names parameter to retrieve all language-dependent descriptions. 
 Application Filter Parameter 
 The endpoint now accepts the optional query parameter application , enabling callers to retrieve a condition type scoped to a specific application: 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/conditiontypes/{conditionTypeId}?application={application} 
 - When application is provided, the condition type is returned for that specific application 
 - When application is omitted, it defaults to the service's configured application context, for example V (Sales) 
 All Language Descriptions ($select=names) 
 A new parameter $select=names has been introduced. When passed, the response includes an additional names array containing descriptions in all available languages. 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/conditiontypes/{conditionTypeId}?$select=names 
 An optional parameter $filter can be combined with $select=names to restrict which language variants are included in the names array. If no $filter is passed, all available language descriptions are returned. 
 Supported syntax: $filter=language IN ('en','de','fr') 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/conditiontypes/{conditionTypeId}?$select=names&$filter=language IN ('en','de','fr') 
 More information will be published with the November release in the API Definition and the Development Guide (Pre-Production). 

 Pricing service - Application Filter and Language Filter on Access Sequence GET Endpoint 
 The GET endpoint for access sequences has been enhanced with an optional application query parameter and a new $select=names parameter to retrieve all language-dependent descriptions. 
 Application Filter Parameter 
 The endpoint now accepts the optional query parameter application , enabling callers to retrieve an access sequence scoped to a specific application. 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/accesssequences/{accessSequenceId}?application={application} 
 - When application is provided, the access sequence is returned for that specific application 
 - When application is omitted, it defaults to the service's configured application context, for example V (Sales) 
 All Language Descriptions ( $select=names ) 
 A new parameter $select=names has been introduced. When passed, the response includes an additional names array containing descriptions in all available languages. 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/accesssequences/{accessSequenceId}?$select=names 
 An optional parameter $filter can be combined with $select=names to restrict which language variants are included in the names array. If no $filter is passed, all available language descriptions are returned. 
 Supported syntax: $filter=language IN ('en','de','fr') 
 GET /api/v1/customizing/accesssequences/{accessSequenceId}?$select=names&$filter=language IN ('en','de','fr') 
 More information will be published with the November release in the API Definition and the Development Guide (Pre-Production). 

 Variant Configuration service - New AVC-Aligned Mode (General Availability) 
 The AVC-Aligned Mode is now available to all customers. Building on the beta version released in 2608 , this release significantly extends the supported AVC syntax and closes key behavioral gaps to SAP S/4HANA for advanced variant configuration (AVC). 
 New syntax functions (2608 + 2611 combined): 
 Numeric: round, nroot, log2, mod 
 String: length, substring, prefix, suffix, to_string, to_int, to_float 
 EXIT / EXIT IF for explicit conditional procedure termination 
 Behavioral alignment with AVC: 
 Set semantics for multi-valued characteristics 
 Automatic inferences in constraints (INFERENCES section no longer required) 
 Symbolic value exclusion via inequality (<>) 
 Negated table inferences (NOT TABLE / FALSE IF TABLE) 
 Sticky static defaults: CT04 defaults always restored when no value is assigned 
 Negative values allowed flag aligned with AVC 
 Preconditions for values of multi-valued restrictable characteristics 
 Procedure termination aligned with AVC (non-terminating on unassigned value) 
 Processing of all dependency types: constraints, procedures, selection conditions, and preconditions 
 Compilation visibility: 
 Compilation errors for unsupported syntax displayed in KB response and at configuration session creation, now persisted in the database 
 Per-dependency compilation status in GET /knowledgebases/{kbId}?$select=dependencies 
 More information will be published with the November release in the AVC-Aligned Mode - Customer Guide (Pre-Production).

title: How fstrim Can Silently Trigger SAP HANA HA Cluster Failovers - A Root Cause Analysis from the Field
author: TaoShen
text:
Abstract 
 A large enterprise customer running SAP S/4HANA on a scale-out SAP HANA database experienced repeated, unexplained Pacemaker HA cluster failovers over a period of several months. Each failover caused a complete business outage affecting mission-critical operations. After an extensive investigation involving SAP, the cloud infrastructure provider, the OS vendor, and the customer's team, the root cause was traced to a seemingly innocuous Linux system utility: fstrim. 
 This article walks through the investigation process, the root cause mechanism, and the resolution — providing actionable guidance for SAP HANA administrators managing HA clusters on Linux. 
 1. System Landscape 
 The affected production landscape consisted of: 
 SAP S/4HANA supporting sales, eCommerce, warehousing, transportation, and finance 
 SAP HANA database in a scale-out configuration 
 SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) with Pacemaker HA cluster (SAPHanaTopology / SAPHana resource agents) 
 XFS file system on NVMe storage via device-mapper (dm) 
 Cloud-hosted infrastructure (IaaS) 
 Third-party endpoint security (real-time antivirus scanning) 
 2. Problem Description 
 Over a span of approximately three months, the production SAP HANA system experienced eight HA cluster failovers. Some required manual intervention to restore operations. Each incident disrupted the customer's entire SAP S/4HANA environment. 
 A critical observation emerged early in the investigation: 
 Nearly all failovers occurred during the same narrow time window each week — the early hours of Monday morning (UTC). 
 This highly regular pattern became the single most important clue in the investigation. 
 3. Investigation 
 3.1 Phase 1: Ruling Out Antivirus Software 
 Because the HANA database servers ran a third-party endpoint security agent with real-time file scanning enabled, the initial hypothesis was that antivirus activity could be interfering with HANA processes or Pacemaker operations. 
 Actions taken: 
 Reviewed the antivirus agent logs for scanning activity on SAP/HANA/Pacemaker directories 
 Added directory-level and process-level exclusions for /hana/shared/*, /usr/sap/*, and Pacemaker paths (per SAP Note 2808515) 
 Completely disabled real-time scanning on a Sunday evening as a controlled test 
 Result: 
 No failover occurred on Sunday night (when fstrim was not scheduled). 
 A failover still occurred on Monday morning — even with antivirus disabled. 
 Log analysis confirmed the antivirus agent was not scanning HANA-related directories during the Monday failover window. 
 Conclusion: The antivirus software was ruled out as the cause of the recurring weekly failovers. (Note: The antivirus agent was separately found to contribute to IPC-timeout-related failovers at other times — a distinct issue addressed in parallel.) 
 3.2 Phase 2: Discovering the fstrim Correlation 
 With antivirus eliminated, the team systematically reviewed all scheduled system activities running during the failover window. The breakthrough came from inspecting the OS systemd timer configuration and system message logs. 
 Key finding: 
 fstrim.timer: configured to run weekly on Monday 
 Window: midnight to 1:00 AM UTC (with ~100 second random delay) 
 Actual observed runtime on production: ~27-30 minutes 
 Actual observed runtime on non-production: ~2 minutes 
 The fstrim execution window overlapped precisely with every recorded failover event. On SLES, fstrim.timer is enabled by default and runs weekly. 
 Immediate mitigation: fstrim was disabled on the production system. From that point forward, no further failovers occurred. The system remained stable for the entire subsequent monitoring period. 
 systemctl stop fstrim.timer 
 systemctl disable fstrim.timer 
 3.3 Phase 3: Understanding the Root Cause Mechanism 
 Disabling fstrim resolved the symptom, but the team needed to understand the technical chain of events — why a storage maintenance utility could trigger a database HA failover. 
 3.3.1 Pacemaker Cluster Monitoring Basics 
 The SAP HANA Pacemaker resource agent (SAPHanaTopology) periodically executes monitoring commands — including hdbnsutil and Python scripts — to verify system replication status and database availability. The key parameters are: 
 60-second timeout. Each monitoring command has a 
 If the command does not return within the timeout, the cluster retries. 
 After multiple consecutive timeouts, the cluster interprets the primary node as unresponsive and initiates a stop/failover action based on the resource agent configuration and replication state. 
 3.3.2 Detailed Failover Timeline 
 Reconstructing a representative failover event from trace files: 
 Table 1: Pacemaker HA Failover Event Timeline (representative incident) 

 Phase 
 Elapsed Time 
 Event 
 Evidence 

 Normal 
 T+0 
 Last successful Pacemaker monitor action (SAPHanaTopology completes in ~6s) 
 Pacemaker log: "end action monitor_clone with rc=0 (6s)" 

 Degraded 
 T+10s 
 Next monitor cycle begins; commands start taking abnormally long 
 hdbnsutil calls no longer returning within expected timeframe 

 Timeout Loop 
 T+10s to T+6min 
 Multiple hdbnsutil / Python calls fail the 60s timeout after repeated retries 
 Each call stuck in process initialization (chmod on trace files) 

 Demotion 
 T+6min 
 Pacemaker demotes the primary DB and issues HANA stop command 
 Cluster resource state transitions logged 

 Failover 
 T+~13min 
 DB stop completes (~7 min); cluster promotes secondary to primary 
 Takeover completed; system back online 
 3.3.3 strace Analysis: Pinpointing the Blocking Point 
 To identify exactly where the monitoring commands were getting stuck, manual hdbnsutil calls were executed during and outside the problem window, traced with strace. 
 Table 2: strace Comparison — hdbnsutil chmod Latency (Normal vs. During fstrim) 

 Scenario 
 Command Traced 
 chmod Duration 
 Total hdbnsutil Runtime 
 Observation 

 Normal period 
 (outside fstrim window) 
 chmod("/usr/sap/<SID>/.../trace/nameserver_*.trc", 0640) 
 0.000012s (~12 μs) 
 ~8 seconds 
 File metadata operation completes instantly; process initialization is trivial 

 During fstrim 
 (within issue window) 
 chmod("/usr/sap/<SID>/.../trace/nameserver_*.trc", 0640) 
 293.055634s (~4.9 min) 
 ~5 minutes 
 OS file metadata operation completely blocked by storage I/O saturation from fstrim 
 The critical insight: hdbnsutil's actual database command executes in milliseconds. The time is spent entirely in process initialization — trace file setup, environment configuration — which depends on OS-level file operations (chmod, write, open). These OS operations were blocked because the underlying storage was saturated by fstrim. 
 Process state captures taken during the fstrim window confirmed the I/O blocking: 
 Table 3: Process State Capture During fstrim Window (ps output summary) 

 Process 
 State 
 Description 

 hdbnsutil (Pacemaker-initiated) 
 D 
 Uninterruptible sleep — blocked in kernel waiting for I/O on /usr/sap/... 

 hdbnsutil (manually initiated) 
 D 
 Same blocking behavior, confirming issue is OS-level, not Pacemaker-specific 

 backint (HANA backup process) 
 D 
 Log backup I/O also blocked; could not write to /usr/sap/.../backint/ 

 fstrim 
 R / S 
 Actively running, issuing discard I/O requests against all mounted file systems 

 Endpoint security agent 
 S 
 Running but idle — real-time scanning already disabled at this point 
 Additional observations during the fstrim window: 
 HANA log backup operations stalled 
 Administrative SSH sessions hung 
 Even basic OS commands (ls, chmod) on affected file systems became unresponsive 
 3.3.4 OS Vendor Kernel-Level Analysis 
 The OS vendor's L3 engineering team analyzed the system core dump and provided a kernel-level explanation of the blocking mechanism: 
 // block/bio.c — submit_bio_wait() 
 // fstrim submits discard requests via this path and waits synchronously 
 int submit_bio_wait(struct bio *bio) { 
 bio->bi_opf |= REQ_SYNC; 
 submit_bio(bio); 
 wait_for_completion_io(&done); // <-- blocks here 
 } 
 The analysis revealed several compounding factors: 
 Severe free-space fragmentation: The XFS file system on the production volume had highly fragmented free space. fstrim with the default minimum block size had to process an enormous number of individual free extents, issuing a discard request for each one. 
 Discard storm: The flood of small discard I/O requests overwhelmed the storage path. Cloud storage backends, in particular, are sensitive to discard storms. 
 Block-layer throttling: The device had blk-throttle (I/O bandwidth throttling) configured. The kernel flag BIO_BPS_THROTTLED on the pending bio confirmed that discards were being rate-limited, further extending fstrim's runtime. 
 I/O path contention: The sustained discard I/O blocked other I/O requests sharing the same storage path — including metadata operations (chmod, write) on the /usr/sap file system where HANA traces and binaries reside. 
 # Key evidence from the core dump: 
 crash> dev -d | grep ff18ba9223888f20 
 254 ff18ba905523d800 dm-3 ff18ba9223888f20 1 0 1 
 # NVMe disk backing dm-3 — the device where fstrim was issuing discards 

 # xfs_trim_extents called with start=0, end=2147475455 
 # processing the entire allocation group in a single sweep 
 4. Root Cause Summary 
 The complete chain of causation: 

 Step 
 What Happens 
 Technical Detail 

 1 
 fstrim runs with default minimum block size 
 On a large production file system with severe free-space fragmentation, this generates thousands of small discard requests. 

 2 
 "Discard storm" + block-layer throttling 
 The flood of discards saturates the storage I/O path. blk-throttle rate-limits the requests, extending total runtime to 20-30 minutes. 

 3 
 OS-level file operations blocked 
 Any process needing file metadata operations (chmod, open, write) on the affected storage path enters D state (uninterruptible sleep), waiting for I/O. 

 4 
 hdbnsutil initialization hangs 
 The HANA utility's startup sequence includes trace file operations (chmod on /usr/sap/…/trace/). A chmod that normally takes microseconds now takes 293+ seconds. 

 5 
 Pacemaker monitoring commands time out 
 Multiple consecutive hdbnsutil calls fail the 60-second timeout. The cluster concludes the primary is unresponsive. 

 6 
 HA failover initiated 
 Pacemaker stops the primary database and promotes the secondary — causing a full business outage. 
 Why was non-production unaffected? On non-production systems, fstrim completed in approximately 2 minutes — well within the Pacemaker timeout window. The production system's larger disk size, higher data volume, more severe free-space fragmentation, and different storage configuration caused fstrim to run 15x longer. 
 5. Resolution 
 5.1 Immediate Mitigation 
 Disabling the fstrim systemd timer immediately stopped the recurring failovers: 
 systemctl stop fstrim.timer 
 systemctl disable fstrim.timer 
 After disabling fstrim, the production system remained fully stable with zero unplanned failovers during the entire subsequent monitoring period (multiple months). 
 Storage snapshot sizes were monitored continuously after disabling fstrim. No significant growth was observed, confirming that disabling fstrim carried no adverse effects on storage efficiency for this environment. 
 5.2 Long-Term Recommendation 
 If fstrim needs to be re-enabled (for example, to optimize storage snapshot sizes), the key is to avoid the "discard storm" by specifying a larger minimum block size: 
 # Recommended: use a minimum discard extent size of 256KB or 1MB 
 fstrim -m 262144 # 256KB minimum 
 fstrim -m 1M # 1MB minimum (skip small fragmented extents) 
 Testing on the DR system confirmed that fstrim -m 1M completed in ~126 seconds (vs. 20-30 minutes with the default setting), with /hana/shared accounting for ~111 seconds and all other file systems completing trivially.

title: Connect to AWS S3 using SAP Cloud Connector for SAP Datasphere Replication flows
author: venkat_madireddi
text:
Introduction 
 When integrating SAP Datasphere with AWS S3, traffic typically traverses the public internet. While TLS encryption protects data in transit, many enterprise security policies require that sensitive data never leave the private network boundary, even when encrypted. AWS Private Link addresses this by routing S3 traffic entirely within the AWS network through a VPC Interface Endpoint, eliminating exposure to the public internet at the network layer. Combined with the SAP Cloud Connector (SCC), this enables SAP Datasphere to access S3 buckets over a SAP Cloud Connector secure TLS tunnel, without any traffic leaving the AWS backbone. 
 This guide walks through the setup and verification of this architecture in a lab / POC-style environment. 
 Disclaimer: This blog is intended for informational and knowledge-sharing purposes only. The configurations described are demonstrated in a SAP lab environment and may not reflect production-ready setups. Please refer to official AWS S3 and SAP documentation. 
 Architecture 

 The key components are: 

 Component 
 Role 

 AWS S3 Bucket 
 Target data store; public access blocked 

 VPC Interface Endpoint 
 Routes S3 traffic privately within the AWS network 

 EC2 Instance 
 Hosts the SAP Cloud Connector; sits inside the VPC 

 SAP Cloud Connector 
 Bridges SAP Datasphere to the private S3 endpoint 
 Prerequisites 
 An active AWS account with the VPC Interface Endpoint for S3 , allowing resources inside the VPC to reach S3 without routing traffic over the public internet. 
 AWS EC2 Instance to host the SAP Cloud Connector 
 An SAP BTP Subaccount for SAP Datasphere (Cloud Foundry environment) 
 1. Provision EC2 AWS instance 
 Provision an EC2 instance inside the same VPC and subnet as the Interface Endpoint. This instance will host the SAP Cloud Connector. 

 Parameter 
 Recommended Value 

 Operating System 
 Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.x or Amazon Linux 2023 

 Instance Type 
 Medium or larger (SCC requires at least 2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM) 

 VPC 
 Same VPC as the Interface Endpoint 

 Subnet 
 Same subnet as the Interface Endpoint 

 Security Group 
 The shared security group that controls access to the endpoint; shared with the EC2 instance 

 Public IP 
 Assign a public IP for initial SSH access 
 2. Verify S3 Access via Private endpoints 
 SSH into the EC2 instance and verify that S3 is reachable through the private endpoint. 
 Install AWS CLI on the Instance ssh -i <your-key.pem> ec2-user@<instance-public-ip>

sudo dnf install -y unzip wget
mkdir -p /data/awscli && cd /data/awscli
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip"
unzip awscliv2.zip
./aws/install
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/bin
aws --version 
 Configure Credentials and Test Access aws configure set aws_access_key_id <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID>
aws configure set aws_secret_access_key <YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY>
export REGION=eu-central-1
# Test standard S3 access
aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket-name

# Test access via the PrivateLink Interface Endpoint DNS
aws s3api head-object \
 --bucket your-bucket-name \
 --key test-file.txt \
 --endpoint-url https://bucket.vpce-<endpoint-id>.s3.eu-central-1.vpce.amazonaws.com 
 A successful response confirms that S3 traffic is routing through the private endpoint. 
 3. Install and configure SAP Cloud Connector 
 Download SAP Cloud Connector 
 Download the SAP Cloud Connector Linux Portable package from SAP Development Tools . The package is a .zip file containing an RPM installer. 
 Transfer the package to the EC2 instance: scp -i <your-key.pem> sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip ec2-user@<instance-public-ip>:/tmp/ 
 Install SAP Machine JRE (Java Runtime) 
 SCC requires Java 17 or 21. SAP Machine JRE is the recommended runtime. wget https://github.com/SAP/SapMachine/releases/download/sapmachine-21.0.5/sapmachine-jre-21.0.5_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
tar zxf sapmachine-jre-21.0.5_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz -C /data/
export JAVA_HOME=/data/sapmachine-jre-21.0.5
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
java -version 
 Install SCC mkdir /data/sapcc && cd /data/sapcc
cp /tmp/sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip .
unzip sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip
rpm -Uvh --force com.sap.scc-ui-<version>.x86_64.rpm 
 Start and Access SCC 
 Once installed, SCC starts automatically as a service and is accessible on port 8443: # Check service status
systemctl status scc_daemon 
 Open a browser and navigate to: https://<instance-public-ip>:8443/ 
 Log in with the default credentials and change the password immediately : 

 Field 
 Default Value 

 Username 
 Administrator 

 Password 
 Manage 
 4. Connect SAP Datasphere Subaccount to SAP Cloud Connector 
 Set Installation Type 
 On first login, select Master as the installation type and save 

 Register the SAP Datasphere BTP Subaccount 
 Login into your BTP Cockpit, navigate to Connectivity → Cloud Connectors → Download Authentication Data 
 You will need to upload the authenticated data file in Step 4 

 2. Login in into SAP Cloud Connector Admin UI https://<instance-public-ip>:8443/ 
 Click Add Subaccount 

 3. Choose to Configure using Authentication data 

 4. Choose from file and browse to select the downloaded file from Step 1- Add subaccount authentication data 

 5. Set L ocation ID you want to use and a Display Name and Finish. 
 6. Verify the connection appears as active in the BTP Cockpit under Connectivity → Cloud Connectors 

 5. Map Virtual Host to the S3 Private Endpoints 
 If you want to prevent your data from being routed publicly through the internet, you can use SAP Cloud Connector as a secure TLS tunnel between the customer virtual private network and SAP Datasphere to privately route the data. Cloud Connector acts as a reverse proxy, create the following system mappings for the regional endpoints where your Amazon S3 bucket is located . you will need to map the virtual host to two separate S3 PrivateLink endpoints for CSV and Parquet files 1. In SAP Cloud Connector, Select SubAccount and choose the Datasphere SubAccount 
 2. Go to Cloud To On-Premise and click the Add button 
 Select Non-SAP System as back-end type 

 3. Set Protocol to TCP 
 4. Set the internal host and port range for Amazon S3 global endpoint for path-syle URL access (for example, s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com) 

 5. Set the Virtual Host and port - must be the same as the internal host and port 

 6. Click Finish to complete endpoint system mapping to enable path-style URL access 

 7. Add endpoint system mapping to enable virtual-hosted-style URL access. Similar to Step 2 to Step 6 
 Go to Cloud To On-Premise and click the Add button 
 Select Non-SAP System as back-end type 

 Set Protocol to HTTPS 
 Set Internal Host and Port - Internal host for Amazon S3 regional endpoint including the name of the bucket that you want to access (for example, <bucket-name>.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com ) 

 Set Virtual Host and Port 
 Hostname must be the same as the internal host and port can be different 

 Deselect Allow Principal Propagation 
 set Host in Request Header to Internal Host 

 Click Finish to complete endpoint system mapping to enable virtual-hosted–style URL access 
 8. Verify the connections for both mappings in SCC 

 6. Add data source location to SAP Datasphere 
 Login in SAP Datasphere and navigate to SYSTEM --> Administration 
 In the Data Source Configuration section add the defined SCC location to the locations list 
 7. Create AWS S3 connection in SAP Datasphere using SAP Cloud Connector 
 1. Login in SAP Datasphere and switch to the HANA<Space> or HDLF <space> to Create a new Connection to AWS S3 in Connection Management 
 2. Click Amazon Simple Storage Service connection in Connection List 

 3. Configure Connection parameters for Amazon Simple Storage with setting the Use Cloud Connector to True 
 Make sure to select the created / corresponding Location for the SAP Cloud Connector instance 

 4. Choose Next and enter connection information and click on Create Connection 

 5. Validate the Connection to verify the connection status 

 With these steps completed, your SAP Cloud Connector is successfully installed, connected, and configured to integrate and create a native connection type of Amazon simple storage service using private endpoints with SAP Datasphere . Now in data builder , you can configure and deploy a Replication Flow with Amazon simple storage service( AWS S3) as source . 
 Conclusion 
 Setting up private connectivity between SAP Datasphere and AWS S3 is straightforward when combining AWS PrivateLink with the SAP Cloud Connector. If you want to prevent your data from being routed publicly through the internet, you can use Cloud Connector as a TLS tunnel between the customer virtual private network and SAP Datasphere to privately route the data. The setup covered in this blog walks through each layer of the architecture: provisioning an EC2 instance inside the VPC to host the SAP Cloud Connector, routing S3 traffic through a VPC Interface Endpoint, and mapping virtual hosts to the private S3 PrivateLink DNS addresses. 

 References: 
 SAP Cloud Connector licensing, download and installation information 
 Amazon Simple Storage Service Connections

title: Post-logoff URL is not validated by UCON
author: anton_lundovskiy1
text:
Hello all, 

 We are investigating a security finding related to post-logoff redirection in SAP CRM WebClient (CRM_UI_START) on an SAP NetWeaver system with SAP_BASIS 7.40. 

 We have activated the UCON HTTP Whitelist and configured Context Type 01 – Trusted Network Zone in Active Check mode. 

 During our analysis, we confirmed that the standard ICF logoff endpoint correctly validates the optional redirectURL parameter against the HTTP whitelist. 

 For example: /sap/public/bc/icf/logoff?redirectURL=https://google.com/ 
 is rejected with: 
 500 Internal Server Error 
 Redirect is not possible 

 We also tested lookalike-domain, userinfo-based and localhost URLs. All were correctly rejected. An explicitly allowlisted URL was successfully accepted. 
 Therefore, the UCON HTTP Whitelist itself is working correctly. 

 However, we identified a different behavior for the standard CRM WebClient Log Off functionality. The CRM callback implementation in: CL_CRM_UI_FRAME
IF_CRM_WEB_CALLBACK~HANDLE_REQUEST
calls:
ir_server->logoff(
 delete_mysapsso2_cookie = abap_true
). 

 The optional REDIRECT_URL parameter is not passed. 

 Consequently, in CL_HTTP_SERVER_NET IF_HTTP_SERVER~LOGOFF redirect_url is initial and the following standard whitelist validation is not executed: IF l_redirect_url IS NOT INITIAL.
 cl_http_utility=>if_http_utility~check_http_whitelist(
 entry_type = '21'
 client = c_client
 url = l_redirect_url
 url_parm_name = 'redirectURL'
 ).
ENDIF. 

 After the session is terminated, CRM WebClient performs the configured post-logoff navigation directly in client-side JavaScript. For example, the generated HTML contains: crmuifClient.winMan.closeAll();
crmuifClient.logOff();
getTopWindow().location.href='<Technical Profile Logoff URL>'; 
 The destination is taken from the Logoff URL configured in the CRM WebClient Technical Profile. Therefore, this post-logoff URL does not appear to pass through the UCON HTTP Whitelist / Trusted Network Zone validation. 

 Relation to SAP Note 1910057 
 We reviewed SAP Note 1910057 – “LOGOFF method: new optional REDIRECT_URL parameter”. 

 The correction introduces the optional REDIRECT_URL parameter for IF_HTTP_SERVER~LOGOFF and moves the HTTP whitelist check for Entry Type 21 into the generic LOGOFF implementation. 

 The corrected implementation performs whitelist check before performing the redirect: cl_http_utility=>if_http_utility~check_http_whitelist(
 entry_type = '21'
 url = l_redirect_url
 url_parm_name = 'redirectURL'
). 

 The Note also states that the purpose of this functionality is to support Web applications that want to display a specific Web page after successful logoff via HTTP redirect. The corresponding correction is present in our system, and we have verified that it works correctly when REDIRECT_URL is supplied. 

 However, the standard CRM WebClient implementation does not appear to use this functionality for its configured Technical Profile Logoff URL. 

 Therefore we have two questions: 
 - What is the SAP-recommended configuration or implementation to ensure that the CRM WebClient post-logoff destination is restricted to approved URLs and cannot bypass the UCON Trusted Network Zone check? 
 - If the current client-side redirect is standard and intended, how does SAP recommend addressing a security requirement that all post-logoff redirect destinations must be validated against an allowlist? 

 We would prefer to use an SAP standard solution and avoid any modification or custom implementation of the CRM WebClient logout functionality. 

 Best regards, 
 Anton Lundovskiy

title: Actual result: Scoring rows are lost after save. in fiori SLC supplier evaluation
author: sanjay-verma
text:
Problem description: 
 For the newly created purchasing category "coal purchase 1" (1), criterion Quantity (02), the header data (Weighting Factor 20.00%) saves and persists correctly. However, the rows entered in the Scoring table (Variance Percentage / Variance Score) do not persist. After saving and reopening the criterion, the Scoring table shows "No data available". 
 Data entered (14 rows, Variance % -> Score): 
 -100 -> 1, -20 -> 10, -15 -> 40, -10 -> 65, -5 -> 80, -2 -> 90, -1 -> 95, 0 -> 100, 2 -> 95, 10 -> 80, 15 -> 60, 20 -> 40, 30 -> 10, 100 -> 1 

 Steps to reproduce: 
 Open F2551, select purchasing category "coal purchase 1", criterion Quantity (02). 
 Choose Edit, add the Variance Percentage / Variance Score rows above. 
 Choose Save. 
 Leave the screen, reopen the same criterion. The Scoring table is empty. 

 Observations and history: 
 - Earlier (03.09.2026 and 08.09.2026) saving in this app failed with a generic "HTTP request failed" message. The ST22 dump was LOAD_PROGRAM_INTF_MISMATCH (interface IF_MDQ_DS_TYPES changed at runtime, terminated in CL_ABAP_BEHV_CTRL). On 08.09.2026 and 14.09.2026 the browser console showed POST /sap/opu/odata/sap/MM_PRC_SEV_CONFIG/$batch returning 403 Forbidden with "Communication error". These were resolved on our side, but the Scoring rows still do not persist. 
 - On every save attempt the browser console logs: submitChanges: "Scoring" is not a deferred group! 
 - Console also shows a missing i18n text for key 'Delete' in bundle prc_sev_confs1 (likely cosmetic). 
 - Unrelated dump seen on 14.09.2026: GETWA_NOT_ASSIGNED in CL_ESH_EXTRACT_SAPSCRIPT_TEXTSCP (Enterprise Search indexing), which we do not believe is related. 

 Expected result: Scoring rows are stored and shown when the criterion is reopened. 
 Actual result: Scoring rows are lost after save. 

 Questions for SAP: 
 Is the "Scoring is not a deferred group" warning a known defect that causes the child Scoring entities to be dropped from the $batch changeset? 
 Is there an SAP Note or correction for F2551 / MM_PRC_SEV_CONFIG that fixes persistence of the variance scoring table? 
 Does the app require a specific authorization or configuration for the child (Scoring) entity that differs from the header entity? 
 Is a customer-side service copy (ZMM_PRC_SEV_CONFIG) supported, or should the standard service be used? 
 System details: 
 - S/4HANA, SAP release 757, development system, client 600 
 - Fiori app: Supplier Evaluation Weighting and Scoring (F2551) 
 - OData service: MM_PRC_SEV_CONFIG (registered as ZMM_PRC_SEV_CONFIG in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, type BEP, co-deployed only, ICF node active)
